newsitem.title: KENYA: Zairean rebels kill, capture Rwandan Hutu leaders. [CORRECTED 15:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels kill, capture Rwandan Hutu leaders. [CORRECTED 15:00 GMT]

text.p: Zairean rebels have either killed or captured and sent back to Rwanda most commanders in the 45,000-strong Hutu army of the previous Rwandan government, a Hutu politician said on Wednesday.

Seth Sendashonga, a former minister in Rwanda's Tutsi-led government now in exile in Kenya, told Reuters the rebels also killed many senior Hutu politicians who served in Rwanda's last government before Rwandan Tutsi rebels seized Kigali in 1994.

"That (Hutu) army has been completely destroyed. Surviving troops are roaming the jungle of Zaire without a command structure and without a political or military objective. The objectives of the Rwandan government have been achieved," Sendashonga said in a telephone interview.
In October the Zairean rebels seized the Zairean border towns of Bukavu, Uvira and Kamanyola, where the commanders and politicians had been living in exile.
He added: "Many more were captured by the rebels, who then turned them over to Rwanda where they are now under arrest."
The Rwandan authorities are likely to try them for their role in the genocide of 1994, when Hutu militants killed about one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Sendashonga, a highly respected Hutu politician and intellectual, said the Hutu army commander, Major-General Augustine Bizimungu, abandoned his forces in Goma and fled to the Zairean capital Kinshasa.
The whereabouts of Bizimungu's deputy, Brigadier-General Gratien Kabiligi, remain unknown, Sendashonga said. Kabiligi was was in charge of operations for the exiled army.
"It has been a complete mess and the Hutu army was completely taken by surprise. Many senior commanders at the rank of colonel were killed when the rebels stormed Bukavu," he said.

Sendashonga said former information minister Eliezer Niyitegeka and former agriculture minister Straton Nsabumukunzi were killed in the rebel attack on Bukavu in October (corrects month) along with former presidential aide Donat Murego. All three men were wanted in Rwanda for their role in the genocide.
Sendashonga said Rwanda's last president before the new government took power in 1994, Theodore Sindikubwabo, left Bukavu some weeks before the rebellion and was now in Kinshasa.
An estimated 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees fled their homeland alongside the Hutu army in 1994 during the genocide.

Most were housed in crowded camps around Goma, Bukavu and Uvira in eastern Zaire, with others in equally crowded camps in western Tanzania. More than 500,000 have gone home since the fighting broke out in eastern Zaire.

In Africa's latest conflict, the Hutu army has been fighting alongside Zaire's ragged and notoriously ill-disciplined army, which has lost most of eastern Zaire to the Rwandan-backed rebel group known as the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL).
The war in Africa's second largest country was sparked by Zairean attempts to expel the Banyamulenge -- an ethnic Tutsi group that came to the area from Rwanda up to 200 years ago.

The Banyamulenge received Rwandan support because of ethnic connections to Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army and also because of Kigali's desire to deal with the threat posed by the exiled Hutu army, regional analysts say.
